# Decision patterns, and a hybrid agent {#sec-ch11}

An experienced cook does not need a recipe for every dish, because most dishes use the same few steps: fry, add water, cook till thick. Software also has such common steps. We call them **patterns**: well-known solutions with a name, so that a team can simply say "put a gate before that action" and everyone understands. In this chapter we collect the patterns for using decision models, and then build an agent with them.

::: {.goals}
- Recognise six common patterns for using decision models in real systems.
- Find a decision step that is wrong even when nothing crashes.
- Divide work correctly between a decision model and an LLM.
:::

![The six patterns in this chapter, as small diagrams. In every one, something else writes or acts, and a typed question decides.](/figures/ch22/catalog.pdf){#fig-catalog}

All six patterns in @fig-catalog follow one rule.

::: {.keyidea}
**The model only answers; your own program takes the action.** The model gives an answer with a probability, and your rules decide what to do with it. So nothing happens without passing through rules you control.
:::

## Six patterns

**1. Extract, then decide.** The input is messy, like an email or a PDF, but the decision is small. LLMs are very good at reading messy text, but weaker at the decision itself. So we let the LLM read the text and fill in a simple form, with fields like "sender", "amount" and "deadline". Then a decision model decides using that form.

![Extract, then decide. The LLM reads the raw text and writes structured fields; a decision model answers a typed question about them; policy thresholds turn the answer into an action. The LLM writes but never decides; the decision model decides but never writes.](/figures/ch22/extract.pdf){#fig-extract}

In our example, extracting first improved the ranking (AUC) from {{< num ch22 llm_decides_auc f2 >}}, when the LLM decided alone, to {{< num ch22 extract_then_jev_auc f2 >}}. But the company's own clean data fields did even better ({{< num ch22 jev_fields_auc f2 >}}), because the alert text never mentions things like how important the computer is. No LLM can extract a fact that is not written. So if clean data already exists, use it.

**2. The decide step.** As Chapter 5 showed, most steps of an agent are small decisions. Give each of these to a decision model as a clear question, and call the LLM only when something must be written. Since every decision comes with a probability, the agent can notice when it is unsure and stop, instead of continuing confidently.

**3. The safety gate.** Before any risky action, such as deleting a file or sending money, ask a clear question: *is this action safe?* Answer it using only facts the attacker cannot change, such as the company's own records. A high probability allows the action, a low probability blocks it, and anything in the middle goes to a person. These are the three doors again, now for actions.

![A guardrail gate. The agent proposes an action. A decision model estimates whether it's safe, from trusted facts only, never from text an attacker could write. High probability allows the action, low probability blocks it, and the middle asks a person.](/figures/ch22/gate.pdf){#fig-gate}

**4. Check the writer.** Some outputs must be written, such as a report or a reply to a customer. After the LLM writes a draft, ask clear questions *about* the draft: is every statement supported by the evidence? Is the tone suitable? Then send it, return it once for correction, or give it to a person. Limit the number of corrections, or the loop may never end.

**5. The router.** To send each case to the right team, ask a pick-one question ("which team?"), but send it automatically only when one team is clearly the most likely. Sending every alert by its top answer sent {{< num ch22 route_all_acc pct >}} to the right team. Sending automatically only when the top probability was at least {{< num ch22 route_line f1 >}} covered {{< num ch22 route_cov pct >}} of alerts, and {{< num ch22 route_acc pct >}} of those went to the right team. The rest went to a general queue for a person to sort.

**6. The memory manager.** Agents keep notes, like a diary, and look things up in them later. Each note and each lookup is a small decision: is this worth remembering? Where should I search? A published system called Jev-Mem uses a System One model for these small decisions and calls a slower, more careful model only to write the final answer; its authors report better and faster answers than the systems they compared it with [@jevmem2026]. Memory mistakes are silent. A fact that was wrongly thrown away is simply missing later, and nothing tells you so. So keep a record of what gets thrown away.

## A hybrid agent

Now let us design the security agent from Chapter 5 as a **hybrid**: a decision model makes every decision, and the LLM writes only what a person will read. Every run leaves a **trace**, a step-by-step record of what the agent saw and what each decision said, with its probability. This one record helps the team find mistakes, answer questions from auditors, and explain any decision later.

![The hybrid agent. A cheap lookup always runs first. Jev decides which other evidence to collect, then answers the three verdict questions together. The policy turns the verdict into an action, and the LLM writes a case note or urgent message only when a person will read it.](/figures/ch24/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-17}

## A mistake with no error message

Suppose we run the agent for a week. Everything looks fine. There are no errors, every answer is readable, and the actions are spread across all three doors. Then we do one simple check that should be done for every decision step of every agent: *count how often each answer is chosen.*

![How often the first version of the agent chose each option at its "which evidence next?" step, across 700 live alerts. It never once chose threat intel.](/figures/ch24/never-picked.pdf){#fig-never-picked}

Across {{< num ch24 n int >}} alerts, the step "which evidence should I collect next?" *never* chose the threat-intelligence lookup, which checks the alert against lists of known dangerous websites and computers, and is the most useful information about an alert (@fig-never-picked). So every verdict was made without it. The ranking quality (AUC) dropped from {{< num ch24 v2_auc f2 >}} to {{< num ch24 v1_auc f2 >}}, and about {{< num ch24 v1_closed_threats_day f1 >}} real attacks per day were closed automatically. Every answer was in a clean, correct format, so nothing in the system complained.

::: {.keyidea}
**Count how often each answer is chosen.** In our example, the agent never once chose the most useful option, and there was no error message. Simple counting is the only way to catch such hidden mistakes.
:::

The fix was not a better model. The threat lookup takes a fraction of a second and costs almost nothing. Deciding *whether* to do the lookup costs about the same as simply doing it. So the agent now always does the lookup. When checking something is cheaper than deciding whether to check it, just check it.

## Hybrid agent against an LLM-only agent

Now compare it with an agent where the LLM makes every decision, using the same steps, tools and thresholds.

![Four measures for the two agents on the same 700 live alerts, scaled to a day. The LLM's stated confidences sent far more alerts to review than the queue can take, so more real threats were never seen by a person.](/figures/ch24/compare.pdf){#fig-compare-17}

The hybrid agent took {{< num ch24 v2_seconds f1 >}} seconds per alert, while the LLM-only agent took {{< num ch24 llm_seconds f1 >}}. The bigger difference is the review queue (@fig-compare-17). The LLM's written confidences are mostly a few round numbers like 0.9 and 0.95, so the lines between the doors cannot separate the cases well, and it sent about {{< num ch24 llm_reviews_day int >}} alerts per day to a team that can review 240. The hybrid sent {{< num ch24 v2_reviews_day int >}}. When the queue is twice too long, the extra alerts are simply not seen. Adding up the attacks that were closed automatically and the attacks that waited in the queue until they were closed unseen, the hybrid missed about {{< num ch24 v2_missed_day int >}} per day, and the LLM-only agent about {{< num ch24 llm_missed_day int >}}.

![Share of each agent's total time spent on each kind of step. In the hybrid, the largest share is the LLM writing for people. In the all-LLM agent, most of the time goes on deciding.](/figures/ch24/labour.pdf){#fig-labour}

@fig-labour shows where the time goes. The LLM-only agent spends most of its time deciding. The hybrid agent spends its biggest share on *writing* notes that people will read, which is the work an LLM does best.

::: {.keyidea}
**Use an LLM for reading and writing, not for deciding.** LLMs are excellent at understanding messy text and writing for people. For the decisions themselves, a decision model is faster, cheaper and more reliable.
:::

::: {.breaks}
All numbers in this chapter are illustrative, including the timings, and part of the difference between the two agents comes from how the example was set up. Treat the speed, the queue and the design lessons as the main findings. Also, every pattern you add is one more place where something can go wrong: if an LLM first reads the text, then a safety check runs, and then a router sends the case on, a mistake can happen at any of these three steps.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Design a safety gate for an email agent that can send messages to customers. What is the clear question, which facts can be trusted, and where are the thresholds?
:::
